Voice AI Engineering · 52 terms

Voice AI glossary.

Plain-language definitions of the terms used across the Voice AI Engineering series — each linked to the article that explains it in depth.

Audio chunk / frame

A short slice of audio, often around 20 ms, sent or processed as one unit so recognition can start before the speaker finishes.

Explained in Article 02 →
Backchannel

Short listener signals such as “mm-hm” or “yeah” that do not mean the person wants to take the turn.

Explained in Article 10 →
Barge-in

The user speaking while the agent is talking. The agent must stop playback, cancel in-flight work and listen, while ignoring noise and short backchannels.

Explained in Article 10 →
Bit depth

The number of bits used to store each audio sample. It sets how many amplitude levels can be represented; 16-bit is standard for speech pipelines.

Explained in Article 02 →
Cascaded pipeline (STT → LLM → TTS)

A voice-agent architecture that chains separate speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis components. It is easier to inspect and control, and streaming lets the stages overlap.

Explained in Article 06 →
Character error rate (CER)

Like WER but measured at character level; useful for spelling patterns and languages where word boundaries are less clear-cut.

Explained in Article 03 →
Code-switching

Switching between languages within one conversation or sentence, such as Arabic with English technical terms. Recognition quality must be tested on it explicitly.

Explained in Article 03 →
Codec (Opus)

An algorithm that compresses audio for transport or storage. Opus is the common choice for real-time voice; it is a different layer from PCM data and from container formats such as WAV.

Explained in Article 02 →
Context window

The amount of text a model can consider in one request. Long conversations need a recent window plus summaries and structured state.

Explained in Article 05 →
Conversation state

Structured, validated task data — dates, choices, approvals — kept alongside the chat history and updated explicitly on corrections.

Explained in Article 05 →
Echo cancellation (AEC)

Removing the agent's own voice, picked up from the speaker, from the microphone signal so the agent does not respond to itself.

Explained in Article 12 →
Endpointing

Deciding where the current speech segment ends, usually from silence duration and recognizer signals.

Explained in Article 09 →
Explicit confirmation

Requiring a clear user “yes” to a read-back summary before executing an action with real consequences, such as a booking or payment.

Explained in Article 13 →
Final transcript

The recognizer's stable result for a speech segment. It ends a segment, but it does not by itself prove that the user's turn is over.

Explained in Article 03 →
Frame processor

A pipeline stage that receives frames (audio, text, control events), transforms them and pushes them downstream or upstream.

Explained in Article 07 →
Human-in-the-loop

Designing the system so a person reviews or approves high-impact decisions, with the AI proposing and the human deciding.

Explained in Article 16 →
Jitter

Variation in packet arrival times. A jitter buffer smooths playback at the cost of a little extra delay.

Explained in Article 08 →
Large language model (LLM)

The component that interprets the transcript, instructions and context, and produces a reply or a tool request. It has no memory beyond what each request contains.

Explained in Article 05 →
NAT, STUN and TURN

NAT hides devices behind shared addresses; STUN helps peers discover a reachable address, and TURN relays media when a direct path is impossible.

Explained in Article 08 →
Noise suppression

Reducing background noise in the input signal. Too aggressive a setting can also remove parts of the speech you need.

Explained in Article 12 →
Observability / tracing

Recording per-turn timings and events across STT, LLM, tools and TTS so you can see where a slow or wrong interaction went off course.

Explained in Article 15 →
P50 / P95 latency

Percentile latency: P50 is the typical case, P95 the slow tail that one in twenty interactions reaches. Voice quality is judged by the tail, not the average.

Explained in Article 11 →
Partial transcript

An early recognition hypothesis that can still change as more audio arrives. Sensitive actions should never be executed on a partial transcript.

Explained in Article 03 →
PCM

Pulse-code modulation: uncompressed digital audio stored as a sequence of sample values, described by sample format, channel count and sample rate.

Explained in Article 02 →
Phoneme

The smallest sound unit that distinguishes words in a language. TTS systems often map text to phonemes before generating audio.

Explained in Article 04 →
PII

Personally identifiable information. Voice agents should collect, log and retain only what the task needs, with consent and access controls.

Explained in Article 14 →
Pipecat

An open-source Python framework for building real-time voice and multimodal agents as pipelines of frame processors.

Explained in Article 07 →
Playback state

Which portion of the generated reply was actually played to the user. After an interruption, history should record only what was heard.

Explained in Article 10 →
Prompt injection

Text from a user, document or tool result that tries to override the agent's instructions. Data must never be treated as instructions.

Explained in Article 14 →
Prosody

The rhythm, stress, pitch and intonation of speech. It strongly affects how natural synthetic speech sounds, and can change meaning.

Explained in Article 04 →
Quality gate

An automated check in the release process that blocks a deployment when evaluation metrics regress beyond agreed limits.

Explained in Article 15 →
Quantization (audio)

Rounding each continuous measurement of a signal to the nearest level that the chosen bit depth can represent.

Explained in Article 02 →
Real-time factor (RTF)

Synthesis (or recognition) time divided by the duration of the audio. Below 1 is faster than real time; it measures throughput, not first-response latency.

Explained in Article 04 →
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

Retrieving relevant documents at answer time and giving them to the model as evidence, so answers rely on your sources rather than memory alone.

Explained in Article 13 →
Sample rate

How many times per second an audio signal is measured, in hertz. 16 kHz is common for speech; a mislabelled sample rate is a classic cause of poor recognition.

Explained in Article 02 →
SLO

Service level objective: a measurable target, such as P95 time to first audio, that defines acceptable behaviour in production.

Explained in Article 15 →
Speech-to-speech model

A model that takes audio in and produces audio out without separate STT and TTS services in the main path. It can use vocal cues such as tone, at the cost of some transparency and control.

Explained in Article 06 →
Speech-to-text (STT / ASR)

Automatic speech recognition: converting spoken audio into text. In real-time agents it usually runs in streaming mode and emits partial and final results.

Explained in Article 03 →
Streaming

Processing and delivering partial audio or text continuously so pipeline stages overlap instead of waiting for complete inputs.

Explained in Article 11 →
Text normalization

Converting written forms such as dates, times, order numbers and abbreviations into speakable words before synthesis.

Explained in Article 04 →
Text-to-speech (TTS)

Synthesizing spoken audio from text. For voice agents, what matters is intelligibility, correct pronunciation of names and numbers, fast first audio, streaming output and immediate cancellation.

Explained in Article 04 →
Time to first audio

The delay from the end of the user's turn until the user actually hears the agent start speaking — the latency people feel most.

Explained in Article 11 →
Time to first token (TTFT)

How long the language model takes to emit its first output token after receiving a request. One stage of end-to-end latency, not the whole of it.

Explained in Article 11 →
Tool calling

Letting the model request an external function — check availability, look up an order — whose result the application executes and validates.

Explained in Article 13 →
Truncation

Removing the unplayed part of an interrupted reply from the conversation history so the model does not assume the user heard it.

Explained in Article 10 →
Trust boundary

A point where data crosses between components with different privileges — for example, from the model to a tool that changes real records.

Explained in Article 14 →
Turn detection

Estimating whether the user has actually finished their turn and expects a reply, combining audio timing with linguistic context.

Explained in Article 09 →
Voice activity detection (VAD)

Detecting whether speech is present in an audio frame. It does not tell you whether the user has finished their thought.

Explained in Article 09 →
Voice AI agent

A system that uses speech as its main interface: it captures audio, works out what the user wants, decides on a reply or an authorized action, and answers with synthesized speech while handling timing, context and interruptions.

Explained in Article 01 →
WebRTC

A browser and native standard for real-time audio and video over UDP, with built-in jitter buffering, echo cancellation and NAT traversal.

Explained in Article 08 →
WebSocket

A persistent, bidirectional TCP connection. Simple for server-to-server audio streaming, but packet loss causes head-of-line blocking on unreliable networks.

Explained in Article 08 →
Word error rate (WER)

The standard ASR accuracy metric: (substitutions + deletions + insertions) divided by the number of reference words, under a documented normalization policy.

Explained in Article 03 →
